summary.simple: The Sun is a star: a huge, glowing ball of hot gas at the centre of our solar system. Its gravity keeps every planet travelling around it.
summary.detailed: The Sun is a yellow dwarf star (type G2 V) that formed about 4.6 billion years ago. It is a huge ball of hydrogen and helium held together by its own gravity, and that gravity holds the whole solar system together.

temperatureContext.simple: About 5,500 °C at the glowing layer we can see, and about 15 million °C deep in the core!
temperatureContext.detailed: The photosphere, the Sun's visible 'surface' of glowing gas, is about 5,500 °C. NASA's fact sheet gives an effective temperature of 5,772 K (about 5,499 °C). The core reaches about 15 million °C.

moons.note: The Sun has no moons. Instead, the planets and their moons travel around it.

composition.simple: Mostly hydrogen and helium gas. There is no solid ground anywhere on the Sun.
composition.detailed: A huge ball of hydrogen and helium held together by its own gravity. In the photosphere, about 91% of the atoms are hydrogen and about 9% are helium. The Sun doesn't have a solid surface like Earth and the rocky planets.

facts.text: The Sun is about 100 times wider than Earth and about 10 times wider than Jupiter.
It would take about 1.3 million Earths to fill the Sun.
The Sun's connection with Earth drives our seasons, ocean currents, weather and climate.
Solar flares are by far the most powerful explosions in the solar system.
